title: An ancient idol drew a $12.7 million bid; Why Turkey failed to get it back
description: A prehistoric marble figurine from Anatolia became the centre of a multimillion-dollar ownership dispute after a reported $12.7 million bid at Christie's. In March 2023, a US appeals court rejected Turkey's attempt to recover the Guennol Stargazer, citing the timing and history of its claim. The case highlights the complex relationship between art-market value, legal ownership and cultural heritage.

title: IRENA Projects Fossil Fuel, Conventional Energy Share Of Jobs To Fall To 16% By 2050
description: Global energy sector employment could reach 343.1 million jobs by 2050 under the Decarbonising Energy Scenario (DES), more than three times the 103.2 million jobs recorded in 2024, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA). The most significant change under the DES is expected to be structural. In 2024, fossil fuels and conventional technologies accounted for approximately 63.4 million jobs, or just over 60% of total energy sector employment. By 2050, their share is projected to decline to around 16% under the DES. Under the Planned Energy Scenario (PES), however, employment in this category is projected to remain considerably higher, at 108.5 million jobs. In contrast, employment in other transition-related technologies is projected to increase sharply from 7.4 million jobs in 2024 to 121.2 million by 2050 under the DES. This category would become the largest contributor to energy sector employment, accounting for approximately 35% of total jobs under the scenario. The shift indicates a transition from a workforce dominated by fossil fuels and conventional technologies towards employment opportunities across a broader range of technologies supporting the energy transition. Energy Transition To Reshape Global Employment Structure The DES envisages a transformation in the composition and geographical distribution of the global energy workforce, supported by increased investment in clean technologies, energy efficiency and supporting infrastructure. Under the PES, global energy sector employment is projected to reach 268.7 million jobs by 2050, more than 70 million fewer than under the DES. The difference is already evident by 2030, when employment is projected to reach 239.6 million jobs under the DES, compared with 178.2 million under the PES. Although employment is projected to grow under both scenarios, the DES is expected to support a larger and more diversified workforce across different time horizons and value-chain segments. The projections highlight the potential for decarbonisation to drive employment growth alongside the transformation of energy systems. Developing Economies To Account For Over 70% Of Energy Sector Jobs Under the DES, global energy sector employment is projected to be heavily concentrated in developing regions by 2050. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to account for the largest share, at 32.5%, followed by East Asia at 21.9%, with China accounting for the dominant share of employment in the latter region. India is projected to account for 18.5%. Together, these regions and countries would represent more than 70% of global energy sector employment. The IRENA report identifies a significant geographical shift in the relative distribution of employment between East Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa by 2050. Several demographic and economic factors underpin this change. Over the coming decades, China's population is expected to decline even as its gross domestic product (GDP) grows, while Africa's population is projected to increase substantially, particularly among younger age groups. Employment intensities in Africa are also significantly higher than in China and East Asia. Consequently, investment demand is more likely to translate into increased employment in Africa, where the capital stock starts from a substantially lower base and takes time to generate higher productivity. The remaining energy sector jobs are projected to be distributed across other regions. The Middle East and North Africa (MENA) and the 'Rest of World' are each expected to account for approximately 6% of employment. Latin America is projected to hold a 5.2% share, followed by Europe at 4.3%, Southeast Asia at 3%, North America at 2.2% and Oceania at 0.3%. These projections underscore the growing importance of Africa and Asia in the global energy workforce, reflecting demographic trends, rising energy demand and the employment potential of energy-transition investments. Europe and North America, by comparison, are projected to account for a combined 6.5% of global energy sector employment. Solar To Lead Renewable Energy Employment Growth Solar energy is projected to become the largest employer within the renewable energy sector, with employment increasing from approximately 7.9 million jobs in 2024 to 38.3 million by 2050 under the DES. Solar would account for nearly half of all renewable energy employment and support 11.7 million more jobs than under the PES in 2050. Bioenergy is expected to be the second-largest contributor to renewable energy employment, with approximately 29.5 million jobs projected under the DES by 2050. Wind energy employment is also expected to expand substantially, increasing more than fivefold from over 1.9 million jobs in 2024 to approximately 11.1 million by 2050 under the DES. This represents 4.9 million more jobs than projected under the PES. The growth is expected to be supported by the expansion of onshore wind and accelerating offshore wind deployment. Hydropower employment is projected to grow more modestly, reaching approximately 4.5 million jobs by 2050. This reflects the maturity of the technology and the declining availability of greenfield project sites. Geothermal energy and other renewable technologies are expected to remain relatively small employers in absolute terms, although they are projected to record rapid percentage growth. These technologies could create niche employment opportunities, particularly in regions with favourable resource endowments.
